constrainterror.description: A ConstraintError is triggered when a cryptographic API is used with parameters that do not comply with security constraints defined in the CrySL rule. These constraints can apply to algorithm selection, key sizes, padding schemes, or cryptographic modes. Such an error indicates that the provided argument violates predefined security policies, which could result in weak encryption, predictable cryptographic outputs, or even insecure configurations that attackers can exploit.

A ConstraintError was triggered due to the use of invalid parameters or transformations in the javax.crypto.Cipher API. This means the current usage violates the defined CONSTRAINTS in the CrySL specification.

Common violations include:
  • Using a key type that is incompatible with the specified transformation
  • Using an unsupported algorithm, mode, or padding
  • Missing or invalid init() calls
  • Calling updateAAD() when it's disallowed
  • Providing incorrect offset or length values that cause array index violations
  • Failing to call getIV() when required by the mode

When calling 
cipherInputStream.read(byte[] data, int offset, int len);
the following constraints must be fulfilled:
  • offset >= 0
  • len > 0
  • length of data >= offset + len

When calling 
cipherOutputStream.write(byte[] data, int offset, int len);
the following constraints must be fulfilled:
  • offset >= 0
  • len > 0
  • length of data >= offset + len
When calling the method setSecure the boolean given must be true.

The constructor looks as follows:
new DHGenParameterSpec(int primeSize, int exponentSize);
examples.solution:
Then the following constraint must be true:
  • primeSize > exponentSize

examples.misuse: The CrySL rule for DHParameterSpec does not contain a constraints section.

While the read method can be called without giving any parameters (it would then only read 1 byte), it can also be called using parameters to specify an array to read to, an offset, and a length:
digest.read(byte[] data, int offset, int len);
examples.solution:
In this case, the following constraints must be fulfilled for each parameter:
  • length(data) >= offset + len
  • offset >= 0
  • len > 0

examples.misuse:
While the write method can be called while only giving a singular byte to write to the output stream, it can also be called using parameters to specify an array of bytes to write, an offset, and a length:
digest.write(byte[] data, int offset, int len);
examples.solution:
In this case, the following constraints must be fulfilled for each parameter:
  • length(data) >= offset + len
  • offset >= 0
  • len > 0

examples._comment: BigInteger is class of java.math package which allows to work with numbers that are too big to fit in standard integer types like int. Cryptographic algorithm require very large prime numbers-often 2048 bits or more and regular int or long max out at 32 or 64bits.
examples.misuse:
Misuse: Using insecure DSA parameters that violate minimum bit-length constraints.

BigInteger p = new BigInteger("123456789"); // Too short
BigInteger q = new BigInteger("12345");
BigInteger g = new BigInteger("67890"); // Too short
DSAParameterSpec spec = new DSAParameterSpec(p, q, g);

This creates a DSAParameterSpec with parameters that do not meet security requirements (e.g., p < 2048 bits).
examples.solution:
Solution: Use strong DSA parameters that meet the minimum 2048-bit requirement.

// Example of generating secure parameters using KeyPairGenerator
KeyPairGenerator keyGen = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("DSA");
keyGen.initialize(2048);
KeyPair pair = keyGen.generateKeyPair();
DSAParams dsaParams = ((DSAPublicKey) pair.getPublic()).getParams();
DSAParameterSpec spec = new DSAParameterSpec(dsaParams.getP(), dsaParams.getQ(), dsaParams.getG());

This ensures that the parameters used in DSAParameterSpec are secure and conform to modern cryptographic standards.

A ConstraintError has occurred due to the use of invalid parameter values with KeyPairGenerator.

This error typically happens when the key size does not match the required value for the selected algorithm, or when an unsupported algorithm is used.

To solve the issue, following constraints must be satisfied:
  • algorithm must be one of: {"RSA", "EC", "DSA", "DiffieHellman", "DH"}
  • If algorithm == "RSA", then keysize must be 3072 or 4096
  • If algorithm == "DSA", then keysize must be 3072
  • If algorithm == "DiffieHellman" or "DH", then keysize must be 3072
  • If algorithm == "EC", then keysize must be 256

While the update method can be called with different sets of parameters, when called as follows:
mac.update(byte[] preInput, int offset, int len);
these contraints have to be fulfilled:
  • length(preInput) >= offset + len
  • offset >= 0
  • len > 0
Similarly, while there are different ways to call doFinal, when using it as below the length of the output array must be greater than outOffset:
mac.doFinal(byte[] output, int outOffset);

The algorithm must be one of:
  • SHA-256
  • SHA-384
  • SHA-512

While the update method can be called with different sets of parameters, when called as follows:
digest.update(byte[] preInput, int offset, int len);
these contraints have to be fulfilled:
  • length(preInput) >= offset + len
  • offset >= 0
  • len > 0
Similarly, while there are different ways to call digest, when using it as follows:
digest.digest(byte[] output, int outOffset, int outLen);
the constraints to be fulfilled follow the same line:
  • length(output) >= outOffset + outLen
  • outOffset >= 0
  • outLen > 0

examples.misuse:
The Signature API is being used with invalid parameters or in an incorrect order, violating the CRYSL rule for java.security.Signature.

Common misuses include:
  • Using unsupported or insecure algorithms (e.g., MD5withRSA)
  • Calling update() before initSign() or initVerify()
  • Providing incorrect offset and len values when working with byte arrays, causing out-of-bounds access

These issues can lead to runtime exceptions, signature failures, or cryptographic vulnerabilities.
